question: Under Civil Code §1185, may a California notary rely on personal knowledge to identify a signer for an acknowledgment?

options.text: No; California requires satisfactory evidence (ID documents or credible witnesses)
options.why: Correct. Civil Code §1185 requires satisfactory evidence (ID documents or credible witnesses); California removed personal knowledge as a method.
Wrong. Other states allow personal knowledge, but California no longer does.
Wrong. There's no relative exception; family members are identified like anyone else.
Wrong. Jurats also require satisfactory evidence in California.

explanation: California notaries must identify signers by satisfactory evidence, not personal knowledge.

question: An ID document used as satisfactory evidence must be current or issued within the last:

options.why: Correct. §1185 accepts an ID that is current or was issued within the last five years.
Wrong. One year is stricter than the law; IDs issued within five years qualify.
Wrong. Ten years is too lenient; the limit is five.
Wrong. There is a time limit: current, or issued within five years.

explanation: Identification must be current or have been issued within five years.

refs.title: Cal. Civ. Code §1185 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 46)

question: Which is acceptable identification in California?

options.why: Correct. A California driver's license is specifically listed as satisfactory evidence in §1185.
Wrong. A Social Security card has no photo or physical description, so it can't identify the person in front of you.
Wrong. Credit cards are issued by private banks and aren't on the §1185 list.
Wrong. Library cards aren't government ID and aren't on the list.

explanation: A California driver's license or state ID card is acceptable satisfactory evidence.

refs.title: Cal. Civ. Code §1185 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 46)

question: Which elements should an acceptable ID contain?

options.text: A photograph, physical description, signature and serial or identifying number
options.why: Correct. Acceptable IDs carry a photo, physical description, signature and serial or identifying number so the notary can match the person.
Wrong. An address alone can't match a face or signature to the person.
Wrong. A fingerprint isn't the standard ID feature the law describes.
Wrong. An employer logo says nothing about identity.

explanation: Acceptable IDs bear a photo, description, signature and identifying number.

refs.title: Cal. Civ. Code §1185 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 46)

question: How many credible witnesses are required if the witness is personally known to the notary?

options.why: Correct. One credible witness is enough if that witness is personally known to the notary and personally knows the signer.
Wrong. Two witnesses are required only when they are not personally known to the notary.
Wrong. California never requires three credible witnesses.
Wrong. When the signer has no acceptable ID, a credible witness is needed.

explanation: One credible witness who personally knows the signer and is personally known to the notary is sufficient.

question: If the credible witnesses are NOT personally known to the notary, how many are needed?

options.why: Correct. Two credible witnesses unknown to the notary must each present satisfactory ID and swear to the signer's identity.
Wrong. One witness is enough only if the notary personally knows that witness.
Wrong. Witnesses must present ID, and three isn't the rule.
Wrong. Without ID, the signer needs credible witnesses.

explanation: Two credible witnesses unknown to the notary must each produce satisfactory ID.

question: Which person may NOT serve as a credible witness?

options.text: Someone named in the document or with a financial interest in it
options.why: Correct. A credible witness must have no financial interest in the document and not be named in it, so their word is impartial.

options.text: The signer's neighbor who has known them for years
options.why: Wrong. A neighbor who knows the signer could qualify if disinterested and meeting the other requirements.
Wrong. A coworker could qualify if disinterested and meeting the other requirements.

options.text: A friend who presents valid ID
options.why: Wrong. A friend with valid ID could qualify if disinterested and meeting the other requirements.

explanation: A credible witness must have no financial interest in, and not be named in, the document.

refs.title: Cal. Civ. Code §1185 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 46)

question: What must a credible witness do?

options.text: Swear or affirm to the notary that the signer is who they claim to be and that the witness has no interest
options.why: Correct. The credible witness swears or affirms that the signer is who they claim to be and that the witness has no interest in the document.
Wrong. Credible witnesses don't sign the document as parties; they vouch for identity under oath and sign the journal.
Wrong. Who pays the fee has nothing to do with the witness's role.
Wrong. If the signer had acceptable ID, no credible witness would be needed.

explanation: Credible witnesses take an oath vouching for the signer's identity.

refs.title: Cal. Civ. Code §1185 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 46)

question: A signer's California driver's license expired last month. It was issued four years ago. Is it acceptable?

options.text: Yes; an ID issued within the last five years is acceptable even if it has expired
options.why: Correct. §1185 accepts an ID that is current or was issued within five years, and this one was issued four years ago.

options.text: No; expired IDs are never acceptable
options.why: Wrong. California expressly allows an expired ID if it was issued within the last five years.

options.text: Only with a credit card as backup
options.why: Wrong. No such pairing exists; the ID either meets §1185 or it doesn't.
Wrong. The same identification rule applies to acknowledgments and jurats.

explanation: An ID qualifies if it is current or was issued within the past five years. What counts is the issuance date, not the expiration date.

refs.title: Cal. Civ. Code §1185 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 46)

question: Is a U.S. passport an acceptable ID?

options.why: Correct. A U.S. passport is listed in §1185 and carries a photo, description, signature and number.
Wrong. It's specifically listed as acceptable.
Wrong. Where the holder lives doesn't matter; any valid U.S. passport qualifies.
Wrong. A passport stands alone; no second document is needed.

explanation: A U.S. passport is satisfactory evidence.

question: Is a driver's license issued by another U.S. state acceptable?

options.why: Correct. §1185 accepts driver's licenses and ID cards issued by other U.S. states.
Wrong. California doesn't limit acceptable licenses to its own.

options.text: Only if the signer lives in that state
options.why: Wrong. The signer doesn't need to live in the issuing state.
Wrong. An acceptable out-of-state license doesn't need a credible witness alongside it.

explanation: Driver's licenses and IDs from other U.S. states are acceptable.

refs.title: Cal. Civ. Code §1185 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 46)

question: What does the California notary's certificate say about identification?

options.text: That the signer was 'proved to me on the basis of satisfactory evidence'
options.why: Correct. California certificates state the signer was 'proved to me on the basis of satisfactory evidence', reflecting §1185.

options.text: That the signer was 'personally known to me'
options.why: Wrong. 'Personally known to me' was removed because California no longer accepts personal knowledge.

options.text: That the signer showed a credit card
options.why: Wrong. Credit cards aren't acceptable ID and aren't referenced in the certificate.
Wrong. The certificate expressly addresses how identity was proved.

explanation: California certificates state the signer was proved on the basis of satisfactory evidence.

refs.title: Cal. Civ. Code §1189 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 48)

question: Where must a notary record credible witnesses?

options.text: In the journal, including each credible witness's signature
options.why: Correct. §8206 requires the journal to reflect credible witnesses, and they sign the journal.
Wrong. Credible witnesses must be documented in the journal.

options.text: On the back of the document
options.why: Wrong. The back of the document isn't a record; the journal is.
Wrong. The certificate alone isn't enough; the journal entry is required.

explanation: Credible witnesses are recorded in the journal and sign it.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8206 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 32)

question: A notary relies on a fake ID that looks genuine and is later sued. What protects the notary?

options.text: Having reasonably relied on ID that appeared genuine, as documented in the journal
options.why: Correct. Reasonable reliance on ID that appears genuine, documented in the journal, is the notary's main defense if the ID turns out to be fake.

options.text: Nothing; the notary is always liable
options.why: Wrong. Notaries who act with reasonable care and document it aren't automatically liable.
Wrong. An employer's liability isn't automatic and doesn't replace the notary's own defense.
Wrong. The bond protects the public, not the notary; the surety can seek repayment.

explanation: Reasonable reliance on ID that appears genuine, recorded in the journal, helps protect a notary from liability.

refs.title: Cal. Civ. Code §1185 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 46)

question: What should a notary do if a signer's ID shows a slightly different name from the document?

options.text: Proceed only if the ID name and the document name reasonably match the same person, and be cautious with any substantial difference
options.why: Correct. Minor variations (a middle initial, a suffix) may be acceptable; a substantial difference means identity isn't satisfactorily proven.
Wrong. Proceeding with a substantial mismatch certifies an identity the ID doesn't support.
Wrong. Notaries never change document contents, including names.
Wrong. Not every difference is disqualifying; small variations can reasonably refer to the same person.

explanation: Names must reasonably correspond; substantial differences mean identity isn't proven.

question: Is identification required for a jurat in California?

options.text: Yes; the jurat form states the signer was proved on satisfactory evidence
options.why: Correct. The California jurat states the signer was proved on the basis of satisfactory evidence, so ID is required.
Wrong. California requires identification for jurats, unlike some states.
Wrong. Every jurat signer must be identified, wherever they live.

options.text: Only if the affidavit is long
options.why: Wrong. Document length has no bearing on the identification requirement.

explanation: California jurats require satisfactory evidence of identity.

refs.title: Cal. Gov't Code §8202 (CA SOS Notary Public Handbook, p. 29)

question: Is a U.S. military ID acceptable identification?

options.text: Yes, if it contains a photo, description, signature and identifying number
options.why: Correct. U.S. military IDs qualify when they have a photo, description, signature and identifying number.
Wrong. A military ID with the required features is acceptable.
Wrong. It may be used for any document, not just veterans' benefits.
Wrong. No commander's letter is needed; the ID itself is enough.

explanation: U.S. military IDs with the required features are acceptable.
